source.title: Instruction Mining: Instruction Data Selection for Tuning Large Language Models
source.authors: Yi-Han Cao; Yanbin Kang; Chi Wang; Lichao Sun

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper varies instruction-tuning data size and reports evaluation-loss outcomes, conceptually testing whether more training samples can worsen test performance. It does not test model-size or epoch sweeps.
record.gate_note: The results relevant to the claim are the OpenOrca data-size sweep and the loss results in Table 3. Other benchmark and instruction-selection results are not rows here because they do not test the double-descent claim. The paper describes the Figure 4 curves in text; exact curve values are not stated.
record.test_reason: The study finetunes LLaMA-2-7B on instruction-data subsets of increasing size and reports evaluation loss. That is a sample-wise test of whether more data can hurt (V3), in a new setting: instruction finetuning of a pretrained LLM. The authors explicitly frame the result as double descent. There is no model-size, epoch, noise or regularization sweep, and no interpolation threshold is identified. T3 fits better than T2 because the novelty is the setting, not a different method for the original question.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors claim a double-descent phenomenon in LLM instruction finetuning: as data size grows, loss first falls, rises after about 10k examples, then improves again. They attribute this to a shift from data quality to data quantity dominating performance, and use it to bound a BlendSearch over data sizes (512–10k). They do not identify an interpolation threshold or test model-size or epoch axes.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies instruction-tuning dataset size for LLaMA-2-7B and evaluates instruction-set losses and benchmark metrics; it does not reproduce the original deep-network model-capacity setup or establish an interpolation threshold.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes vary by dataset (OpenOrca versus Dolly), data-selection method (quality-selected versus random), and evaluation metric (SELF-INSTRUCT versus MT-BENCH loss).

fits_no_version.finding: The quality-selected and random-data loss curves converge and intersect as data size grows (Phenomenon 2). The authors read this as data quality mattering less at larger sizes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The benefit of quality-based data selection shrinks as finetuning data size grows.

record.peer_reviewed: Published as a conference paper at COLM 2024
record.problems: The core data-size analysis uses LLaMA-2-7B on OpenOrca; the interpolation threshold is not measured. Exact values for the Figure 4 curves are not stated in the text, and no uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying Table 3 size-and-loss results were left out. Other benchmark and model-comparison results were omitted because they do not directly measure the double-descent data-size claim.

untested.parts: No model-size sweep. Only 7B, with 13B used in a separate robustness check, not a capacity sweep.
No epoch or training-time sweep; all runs use 3 epochs.
No interpolation threshold is measured or located; the peak near 10k examples is not tied to fitting the training set.
No capacity sweep across model classes.
No effective-complexity measure predicting peak location.
No label-noise, regularization or multiple-peak analysis.

missing.what: OpenLLM benchmark scores by data size: Selected 10k avg 58.65 vs 40k 59.25; Random 58.74 vs 58.95. ARC falls 56.66 to 54.44 (Selected); MMLU rises.
Location of the loss peak (around 10k examples) and the shape of the second descent in the Figure 4 sweep; only text description available, no values.

record.verdict_notes: This is a data-selection methods paper; the double-descent observation is secondary and rests mainly on Figure 4, whose curve values are not given in the text. Table 3 does not show a second descent: 90k loss exceeds 20k loss under both sampling methods. That conflicts somewhat with the text's claim of later improvement. No uncertainty or seeds are reported, and many differences are within a few thousandths of loss. Finetuning a pretrained 7B model for 3 epochs on up to 90k examples is unlikely to involve interpolation in the original sense, so the link to V3's mechanism is loose.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size sweep or interpolation threshold by model size.
No epoch- or training-time sweep; the estimation and ablation settings use three epochs.
The paper varies training-data size and evaluates loss, but does not establish that the loss rise occurs near a measured interpolation threshold.
No capacity sweep across model classes or general risk-versus-capacity test.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as predicting peak locations across axes.
No test of label-noise or regularization dependence, multiple peaks, or optimally tuned regularization.
No re-counting of complexity by effective parameters or test of whether that turns the curve into an ordinary U-shape.

relationships.condition: LLaMA-2-7B instruction finetuning on OpenOrca (and, more weakly, Dolly); SELF-INSTRUCT and MT-BENCH evaluation loss
relationships.reason: The authors state loss rises after about 10k examples and later improves (r29, r30, Figure 4 described in text only). Table 3 shows higher loss at larger sizes (r2, r3, r7, r10, r14, r17, r24, r28).
relationships.display_finding: Evaluation loss rose after about 10,000 examples and later improved, with larger training sets also yielding higher loss in tabulated comparisons.

relationships.condition: Magnitude of the rise and choice of metric
relationships.reason: Several rises are tiny (about 0.002–0.005 loss) with no uncertainty reported (r11, r13, r21). relationships.display_finding: Some loss increases are only about 0.002–0.005 without uncertainty estimates; from 10k to 40k examples, OpenLLM average and MMLU improve while ARC declines.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: OpenOrca data-size sweeps, especially the reported evaluation-loss curves
reader_labels.reason: The authors describe loss rising as data size increases after around 10,000 examples, before improving again at larger sizes; Table 3 also has higher loss at larger sizes in several comparisons (r2-r3, r7, r10-r11, r13-r14, r17, r21, r24, r28-r30). This supports the claim that more data can hurt, but not the asserted location near an interpolation threshold.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Dolly data-size results and random OpenOrca SELF-INSTRUCT loss comparison
reader_labels.reason: Some larger-data comparisons instead have lower loss, and the loss trajectories are not uniformly rising across datasets or sampling methods (r6, r16, r20, r23, r27). The paper does not measure an interpolation threshold.
